analysis.one_liner: Raises estate and gift taxes on the largest fortunes, up to 65% on billion-dollar estates.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee: it was introduced in April 2023 with 2 cosponsors and never received a vote, a committee hearing, or any further action before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would tax the transfer of very large fortunes more heavily. Estates worth over $1 billion would face a 65% tax rate, and the amount of an estate exempt from tax would drop from about $13 million to $3.5 million [S2][S3]. It would also close several trust and valuation techniques that wealthy families use to shrink their taxable estates, while loosening the rules for family farms and conservation easements [S2][S3]. The bill never got past its first step: it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and sat there for the rest of the Congress [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit indirectly, because taxing the largest estates more heavily raises federal revenue that can otherwise be used for public priorities or lower deficits. Family farms and ranches get direct relief: the special farmland valuation break rises from $750,000 to $3 million, making it easier to keep a farm in the family without a large tax bill [S3]. Landowners who donate conservation easements get a bigger exclusion ($2 million instead of $500,000) and a larger deduction percentage (60% instead of 40%) [S2][S3]. Heirs and recipients of estates and gifts would also get new disclosure of what each interest they received was valued at [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Estates over $1 billion would be taxed at 65%, and new brackets would apply 45% above $3.5 million, 50% above $10 million, and 55% above $50 million, raising revenue from the largest transfers of wealth [S2][S3].
The basic estate tax exclusion would drop to $3.5 million, meaning far fewer estates would escape the tax entirely under the much larger current exemption [S2][S3].

The bill restricts grantor retained annuity trusts (a freeze technique that lets asset appreciation pass to heirs tax-free) by requiring a minimum 10-year term and a minimum remainder value, and applies transfer taxes to assets held in grantor trusts [S2][S3].

It limits the 'valuation discounts' that let families claim their shares of a family business are worth far less than the underlying assets, and disallows step-up in basis for property held in certain grantor trusts [S2][S3].

The farmland valuation break rises from $750,000 to $3 million with inflation adjustment, and the conservation easement exclusion rises to $2 million with a 60% applicable percentage, easing the burden on farm and land conservation estates [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Estates and their heirs: the tax falls on decedents' estates worth more than $3.5 million after the change, with the steepest new rates on estates above $50 million and $1 billion. Wealthy gift-givers also face tighter annual exclusion limits for certain transfers (like transfers in trust and illiquid interests), and owners of grantor trusts would owe transfer tax on assets that currently escape it [S2][S3]. The estate planning industry — lawyers, trust companies, and advisors who sell these techniques — would lose a large share of its market.
analysis.who_pays_short: Estates over $3.5 million and their heirs

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes real compliance burdens: it requires consistent basis reporting for gifted property and trust transfers, and requires executors and donors to disclose detailed valuations of each interest to Treasury and to every recipient [S2][S3].

Critics of higher estate taxes argue that the 65% top rate and the much lower $3.5 million exemption discourage saving and can force heirs of illiquid family businesses to sell assets to pay the tax, though the bill does raise the farmland and conservation carve-outs substantially to blunt that concern for farms and ranches [S3].
The valuation and trust rules are technical and would require regulations to administer, adding complexity for taxpayers and the IRS alike [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets its heaviest rates at the very largest fortunes (65% above $1 billion) while actively easing the burden on family farms and conservation donors, which addresses the most common objection to estate tax increases. The main costs — complexity, compliance paperwork, and a lower exemption that could touch more mid-sized estates — are real but modest compared with the revenue raised from the largest transfers of wealth. The main honest caveat is that the bill's revenue depends on whether the anti-avoidance rules hold up against a well-resourced planning industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders, joined by Senator Elizabeth Warren, introduced the bill on April 18, 2023 [S3].
On the same day it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance [S5].
The bill attracted 2 cosponsors, both Democrats [S4].
No further action appears in the legislative record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The owners of the largest estates and the wealth-planning industry are better off, because the current low estate tax exemption and the trust and valuation techniques the bill targets remain untouched. The bill's sponsors and the broader public gain nothing, since no revenue is raised and no vote was ever taken.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the For the 99.5 Percent Act to raise estate and gift taxes on the largest fortunes and close trust and valuation loopholes.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Joined Sanders in introducing the bill.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Senate committee chaired by Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in April 2023 and took no action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remaining 20 months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The only Senate supporters in the record are one Independent and two Democratic cosponsors; no Republican supported it, and the Democratic-run Finance Committee did not advance it either.

industries.note: Estates above $3.5 million would face higher rates, up to 65% above $1 billion, and the trust and valuation techniques used to shrink taxable estates would be curtailed. Their interest in keeping the current system is directly at odds with the revenue ordinary taxpayers would otherwise gain.

industries.industry: Estate planning, trust, and wealth advisory industry
industries.note: The bill's core purpose is to shut down specific planning products — short-term GRATs, grantor trust sales, minority-interest discounts, GST-exempt dynasty transfers — that this industry sells to wealthy families. Its revenue depends on keeping the avoidance channels open.
The special farmland valuation reduction rises from $750,000 to $3 million with inflation adjustment, making it substantially easier for farm estates to escape the tax [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Land conservation and conservation easement donors
industries.note: The estate tax exclusion for land subject to a conservation easement rises to $2 million (from $500,000) and the applicable percentage rises to 60%, a direct incentive to conserve land.
